title: Lesson 1: From Consultant to Principal
description: The shift that defines a principal: from selling your own skill to building a delivery system. Why the unit of output changes, how leverage replaces hours, and what you have to stop doing to operate at scale.

questions.question: A client asks who will actually do the work. Which answer marks a principal rather than a consultant who employs staff?
options: I will, and I will stay on it personally until it is done.
The practice will: the method, the playbook, and the staffed team carry it.
A contractor will, and I will check in at the end.
Whoever is free, and I will supervise every step closely.
questions.explanation: A principal sells capacity and points at the delivery system, so the result does not depend on any one person's hands being on the work.

questions.question: In a knowledge practice, what does codification accomplish?
options: It raises the hourly rate the practice can charge its clients.
It keeps the method inside the principal's head for tighter control.
It turns the judgment used to do the work into a repeatable system others can run.
It removes the need for judgment from every part of the work.
questions.explanation: Codification captures the small decisions an experienced person makes automatically so a competent executor can run them without the original expert in the room; judgment is reserved for the moments that truly need it.

questions.question: As a practice grows from one engagement to many, how does the principal's focus shift?
options: From a single project's outcome to the health of the whole portfolio.
From the quality of each deliverable to the size of the team.
From delivery risk to the marketing of new service lines.
From billable hours to the number of clients on the roster.
questions.explanation: A portfolio is made or broken by the pattern across engagements, such as utilization, margin, and concentrated risk, not by any single project.
